It argues that deep responsibility is not limited to the moral, and that attributability and accountability are independent, not two levels. Accountability may need nothing metaphysically robust. Limits: the positive view is offered as a hunch, the psychopath is a stipulated case, and the lecture does not restate the Reason View of Freedom Within Reason ([LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md)). |
| [LIT-1210](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1210.md) v2 | Natural Moralities: A Defense of Pluralistic Relativism | Wong (2006). There is no single true morality, but there can be several true moralities, each answering the same problem of how to live well together under a common core of human values; pluralistic relativism sits between universalism and "anything goes". | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-18, not read. A lawful full text was sought on 2026-10-29 and not reached. OpenAlex reports the book closed, with the Oxford Academic DOI as its only location; the publisher offers it only to subscribers, and web searches found only catalogue, review and paid e-book listings, and no author or repository copy. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-1370](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1370.md) v2 | Pluralistic ignorance and alcohol use on campus: Some consequences of misperceiving the social norm | Prentice and Miller (1993). Princeton students believed their peers were more comfortable with campus drinking practices than they were themselves; over time men's private attitudes shifted toward the misperceived norm, while women's alienation from it grew. | Unavailable — no lawful copy reached, 2026-10-22; failed on availability. The article is closed: Unpaywall and OpenAlex report no open copy and no repository full text; the APA PsycNET copy is paywalled; the authors' institutional pages (Princeton's research portal, two records; Stanford GSB's publication page for Dale Miller) list it without a file; PubPeer has a record only. A web search found no author's copy. The summary is the abstract's and the paper's standard reading, unchecked. Registered from the owner's exchange of 2026-10-22, "Graph Learning Applications". | [LIT-1402](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1402.md) v2 | The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin | Franklin (written 1771–1790; first published 1791). The memoir of his life to 1757. Part Three holds the anecdote the Benjamin Franklin effect is named for: to win over a hostile new member of the Pennsylvania Assembly, Franklin asked to borrow a scarce book from his library, returned it with thanks, and the man thereafter spoke to him with civility and "manifested a readiness to serve me on all occasions". Franklin gives it as "another instance of the truth of an old maxim", "He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged", and as a lesson in prudence. Around it the memoir is a record of how he got others to act with him: undogmatic speech, projects presented as his friends', and opinion prepared in print and through the Junto's satellite clubs. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1360.md)) in full, from Project Gutenberg eBook [#148](https://github.com/dmarx/nucleation/issues/148) (Harvard Classics, 1909); worth reading as the source of the Benjamin Franklin effect and, around it, a first-hand manual of influence: modest speech, projects put forward as "a scheme of a number of friends", opinion prepared in print and spread through the Junto's clubs "as arising in each of them". Read it knowing that it is a memoir written decades after the events, for posterity and in part from memory without papers; that the borrowed-book story is one instance of an "old maxim", given as prudence, with the member unnamed and the effect reported by the man who sought it; and that the edition's chronology list has errors the memoir itself contradicts. |
| [LIT-1408](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1408.md) v4 | Intergroup Contact Theory | Pettigrew (1998). Reviews Allport's contact hypothesis (equal status, common goals, cooperation, authority support) and names four problems: selection bias in cross-sectional studies, an expanding list of conditions that are facilitating rather than essential, no account of process, and no account of how effects generalize. Proposes four processes (learning about the outgroup, changed behaviour as the precursor of attitude change, affective ties, and ingroup reappraisal, whose outcome it calls "deprovincialization"), three sequential strategies for generalization (decategorization, salient categorization, recategorization), and a longitudinal contact theory in which Allport's four conditions and a fifth, friendship potential, are essential and other factors facilitating. In the author's European surveys the path from outgroup friendship to less prejudice is stronger than the reverse. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1408.md)) in full, from an Annual Reviews PDF of the chapter on Serendip Studio, Bryn Mawr College's science-education site (https://serendipstudio.org/oneworld/system/files/annurev.psych_.49.1.65-2.pdf); worth reading as the review that turned Allport's contact hypothesis into a theory with four processes (learning, changed behavior, affective ties, ingroup reappraisal), a staged account of generalization and a fifth condition, friendship potential. Read it knowing that its processes are proposed rather than tested, that its causal evidence is mostly the author's cross-sectional European surveys, that "deprovincialization" occurs once and rests on one unpublished analysis of national pride, and that its model still treats Allport's four conditions as essential, which the 2006 meta-analysis ([LIT-1413](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1413.md)) does not bear out. |
| [LIT-1413](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1413.md) v3 | A Meta-Analytic Test of Intergroup Contact Theory | Pettigrew & Tropp (2006). A meta-analysis of 515 studies (713 independent samples, 250,089 participants, 38 countries, through 2000) finds that intergroup contact typically reduces intergroup prejudice (random-effects r ≈ −.21; 94% of samples negative). Samples without choice of contact show larger effects, and the more rigorous studies larger ones (experiments −.34), though for racial and ethnic targets experiments show no advantage. Five of six publication-bias checks find none; Vevea and Hedges's model, adjusted, leaves no significant overall effect but a significant one for well-controlled designs. Effects generalize to the whole outgroup and, in few tests, beyond. Allport's optimal conditions enhance the effect (structured programs −.29 against −.20) but work as a bundle and are not essential to it. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1407.md)) in full, from the published article's PDF on a University of Pennsylvania Wharton site (https://ideas.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Pettigrew-Tropp.pdf); worth reading as the meta-analysis of 515 studies (713 samples) that established a reliable negative association between face-to-face intergroup contact and prejudice (r ≈ −.21, −.34 in experiments) and showed Allport's conditions to enhance it without being needed. Read it knowing that most of its samples are cross-sectional surveys of reported contact, that one of its six publication-bias checks (Vevea and Hedges) leaves no significant overall effect, and that the larger effects of rigorous designs come from non-racial targets: for racial and ethnic samples experiments give −.22, the overall mean. |
| [LIT-1419](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1419.md) v2 | Liking a Person as a Function of Doing Him a Favour | Jecker & Landy (1969). The first experimental test of the Benjamin Franklin effect. Participants won money in a concept-formation task; afterwards one group was asked by the experimenter to return it as a personal favour (he was paying out of his own pocket), one was asked by a departmental secretary on behalf of the psychology department, and one was not asked. Those who did the experimenter a personal favour rated him most likable. Standardly read as a dissonance effect: one justifies a favour by liking its recipient. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-23, not read. A lawful full text was sought on 2026-10-29 and not reached. OpenAlex reports it closed with no repository copy; the SAGE page is paywalled; a web search found only secondary accounts and abstract listings (Scilit). It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, and its summary remains secondary. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1427](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1427.md) | Psychopathy: A Clinical Construct Whose Time Has Come | Hare (1996), Criminal Justice and Behavior 23(1):25–54. The programmatic statement that psychopathy, once reliably measured by the PCL-R, is a clinical construct of real use to the criminal justice system, including for predicting recidivism and violence. Unread: the author's ResearchGate copy refused this client. The construct is read in Hare & Neumann (2008). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 from Crossref, not read: a lawful copy exists but this client could not fetch it, so this failed on access, not availability. A full-text PDF is linked from the author's ResearchGate profile (publication 280798957, under profile/Robert-Hare-2), apparently his own upload, but ResearchGate answered every request with HTTP 403, so neither the file nor its uploader could be confirmed. Unpaywall and OpenAlex report no open copy, the journal (SAGE) is closed, and the author's own site, hare.org, lists the paper with a DOI link and no PDF. The construct it presents is read first-hand in Hare and Neumann's 2008 review ([LIT-1428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1428.md)), which gives the PCL-R items, their four factors and their two-factor grouping. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied or ResearchGate can be reached, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1428.md) | Psychopathy as a Clinical and Empirical Construct | Hare & Neumann (2008), Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 4:217–246. The PCL-R's items form four correlated factors, Interpersonal, Affective, Lifestyle and Antisocial, explained by one superordinate factor; psychopathy is dimensional, and no component, affective or antisocial, is more essential than the others. Cleckley's Clinical Profile, drawn from an unrepresentative sample, should not be the test of the construct. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1094](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1094.md)): in full, from the copy Hare posts on his own site. Worth reading as the authors' own statement of what the construct is, made while defending it against the charge that the PCL-R has "drifted" from Cleckley. The PCL-R's 20 items fall, 18 of them, into four correlated factors: Interpersonal and Affective (together Factor 1) and Lifestyle and Antisocial (together Factor 2). A single superordinate factor explains them, and the authors hold that no component, the affective one included, is more essential than the others. That is the sharpest constraint the record has on borrowing only the affective features of psychopathy for a corporation. Hare receives royalties from the PCL-R. |
| [LIT-1683](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1683.md) | Unto Others: The Evolution and Psychology of Unselfish Behavior | Sober & Wilson (1998). Part I defends multilevel (group) selection as a cause of evolutionary altruism; Part II argues that the case for psychological egoism fails and that natural selection likely produced genuinely other-directed ultimate desires, distinguishing evolutionary from psychological altruism. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. The Internet Archive's copy (untoothersevolut00sobe) is for print-disabled readers only and is not lent, and no open edition was found. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Stich 2006 ([LIT-1737](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1737.md)). |
| [LIT-1713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1713.md) | Responsibility to Future Generations: A Moral Reframing Strategy for Combatting Climate Change | Syropoulos, Kraft-Todd, Mah, Markowitz & Young (2023). Thirteen studies (six main, seven supplementary; N = 161,633) on felt responsibility to future generations (RFG). In Eurobarometer data from 34 European countries (N = 109,513), a majority in 33 agreed "We need to reform to benefit future generations even if that means making some sacrifices now"; agreement barely related to ideology, age or gender (meta-r .03 to .07) and weakly to subjective status (.13). In US samples RFG was endorsed more than responsibility to reduce one's own contribution to climate change (RCC), correlated with conservatism half as strongly (meta-r −.21 against −.45), and predicted self-reported proenvironmental behaviour, concern and policy support. In a preregistered experiment (N = 3,175), five brief interventions (a letter to a person born today, legacy reflection, reflection on past generations' sacrifices, a park video, a 385-word excerpt of *What We Owe the Future*) each raised RFG and proenvironmental intentions by small amounts (d = .14 to .54); only the letter raised donations. Reflection on past sacrifices raised RFG but not RCC. All outcomes are self-reports or a small donation. **status_note**: worth reading as the largest study of felt responsibility to future generations, its spread and its political neutrality, and as the record's only experiment comparing legacy, reciprocity, a particular future person and an impersonal longtermist text as routes to it; read in place of Syropoulos and Markowitz 2021. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1293](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1293.md)), in place of [LIT-1741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1741.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the largest study of felt responsibility to future generations, its spread and its political neutrality, and as the record's only experiment comparing legacy, reciprocity, a particular future person and an impersonal longtermist text as routes to it; read in place of Syropoulos and Markowitz 2021. |
| [LIT-1717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1717.md) | Leaving a Legacy: Intergenerational Allocations of Benefits and Burdens | Six experiments (N = 76, 101, 64, 32, 131, 92; U.S. undergraduates, MBA students and university staff) on how the valence of what is passed on affects concern for one's legacy and generosity to future others. Framing climate change as leaving burdens, rather than using up benefits, raised a generativity scale built from items about being remembered and living on (4.90 vs 4.10), direct concern with one's legacy, felt responsibility and affinity toward future generations, and ethical concern; recalling one's own past burden allocation raised moral emotions. In allocation tasks people favoured themselves more with benefits than with burdens. The difference appeared only when the recipient was in the future (not in a dictator-game version with a present recipient), and only when the allocator was a party to the trade-off (not when allocating between two other people). One item on ethical considerations statistically accounted for the first of these. The authors read the pattern as legacy concern, which they define as the wish to extend the self beyond death, engaged more by leaving burdens than by withholding benefits. Legacy concern was measured only in the attitude studies, never in the allocation studies. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1273](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1273.md)), in place of [LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the legacy programme's fullest experimental statement before the 2012 mortality studies, and as the record's only second-hand source for Wade-Benzoni 2006 ([LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md)). Read it knowing that legacy concern and generosity are never measured in the same study, and that the generosity effects sit in one cell: people keep more benefits for themselves when the other person will receive them later. |
| [LIT-1729](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1729.md) | Empirical Approaches to Altruism | The SEP survey of the empirical egoism–altruism debate, revised in 2025. On the standard account, altruism needs an ultimate desire for another's well-being; biological and social-science senses of "altruism" settle nothing about it. Batson's experiments make a strong case against the aversive-arousal and social-punishment versions of egoism. Self-other merging is a different challenge: only numerical identity with the helped person would make helping egoistic, and none of the four measures used by Cialdini et al. and Batson et al. (IOS, "we", perceived similarity, trait-rating difference) tests for it. The authors report that Batson et al. (1997) avoided Cialdini's methodological problems and found empathy's role "clearly evident", and that a preregistered study (N = 680) supports the empathy–helping link. Altruism is still not shown: divine punishment, principlism, non-moral norms, and habitual or Pavlovian helping remain to be ruled out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1274](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1274.md)), in place of [LIT-1700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1700.md) and [LIT-1728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1728.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the shortest neutral account of the 1997 merging exchange the record holds: it quotes both papers' measures, and it argues that a merging criterion must be one of numerical identity to matter for egoism. It does not report the 1997 results in numbers. |
| [LIT-1743](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1743.md) | Preregistered Replication and Extension of “Moral Hypocrisy: Social Groups and the Flexibility of Virtue” | Robertson, Akles & Van Bavel (2024). Two preregistered experiments (minimal groups n = 590; partisans n = 577) did not replicate intergroup moral hypocrisy; the minimal-group contrast is statistically equivalent to zero. In minimal groups, in-group favouritism in fairness judgments rose with collective identification and was not significant overall (p = .07); partisans judged out-party members' identical selfish acts less fair (p = .003). | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1245](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1245.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript on OSF; worth reading as the record's only preregistered evidence on minimal-group favouritism. Valdesolo and DeSteno's intergroup moral hypocrisy did not replicate; minimal-group favouritism appeared only as it rose with identification, and partisans derogated the out-party. |
| [LIT-1748](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1748.md) | The Psychology of Existential Risk: Moral Judgments about Human Extinction | Schubert, Caviola & Faber (2019). Five studies (N = 2,507 as stated) of Parfit's three outcomes: no catastrophe, 80% of humanity killed, 100% killed. Most laypeople judge extinction bad and say it must be prevented, but only 19–37% of those ranking the outcomes in the expected order judge the step from 80% to 100% worse than the step from none to 80%. More do when the victims are zebras, when the catastrophe sterilizes rather than kills, or when told to consider the long-term future (39–50%). A majority (67–77%) do only when told the surviving future would be long and utopian. People recruited as existential-risk mitigators do so unprompted (86%). The authors conclude that laypeople attend to immediate harm to fellow humans and neglect the long-term consequences. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1270.md)) from the publisher's PDF (CC BY), without the supplementary materials; worth reading as the first experiment on how far lay moral concern reaches past the living, and what makes it reach further: salience of the future, its quality, and less sympathy with the victims. |
| [LIT-1749](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1749.md) | Population ethical intuitions | Caviola, Althaus, Mogensen & Goodwin (preprint 2021; Cognition 2022). Nine experiments (N = 5,776 as stated) on lay population axiology. For a fixed population to be better existing than not, people require more happiness than suffering: about 75% happy people, still about 61% when the two are stated to be exactly equally intense. Yet adding one extremely happy person to a world is judged as good as adding one extremely unhappy person is bad, so people reject neutrality and the procreation asymmetry. They prefer larger happy and smaller unhappy populations when averages are fixed, but the preference for more happy people fades and reverses at a billion. With totals fixed they prefer higher averages, and in conflicts averagism tends to win, even favouring adding near-maximally unhappy people who raise the average. Prompts to reflect move judgements toward totalism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1267.md)) from the authors' PsyArXiv preprint (osf.io/wdbr8, OSF file of 2021-04-01); worth reading as the main experimental evidence on whether ordinary judgement is person-affecting or impersonal about merely possible people, and on how weak its totalism is at large numbers. |
| [LIT-1766](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1766.md) | Recategorization and Prosocial Behavior: Common In-Group Identity and a Dual Identity | A review of the common in-group identity model applied to helping. Recategorizing two groups as one removes in-group bias in helping: in a laboratory study, help to an original out-group member rose to the in-group level; at a football stadium, White fans complied with a Black interviewer's request more often when he wore their university's hat (59% vs 36%). Commons-dilemma studies show the same for cooperation. But the form of the shared identity matters. White students helped a Black student least when he called himself a Black person or a Black Colgate student (a dual identity), and most when he called himself a Colgate student. In the second study, empathic concern partly mediated that effect on helping; attitudes did not. The authors trace the dual identity's cost to majority members projecting their group's standards onto the superordinate category, and to identity threat. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1286](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1286.md)), in place of [LIT-1710](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1710.md) and [LIT-1709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1709.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the model's authors' own account of how an enlarged "we" extends helping across group lines, with the qualification that the "we" which helps is the helper's version of it. |
| [LIT-1786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1786.md) | Group-level self-definition and self-investment: A hierarchical (multicomponent) model of in-group identification | In-group identification has five components on two correlated dimensions. Group-level self-definition is individual self-stereotyping (seeing oneself as like the average member) and in-group homogeneity; group-level self-investment is solidarity, satisfaction and centrality. In confirmatory factor analyses of Dutch, European and university identification in two cohorts (N = 464, 363), this model fit better than one-factor, two-factor and cognitive-versus-affective alternatives; the two dimensions correlated .61 to .77. Prospectively, the components predicted different things: centrality predicted perceived threat, homogeneity perceived intergroup difference, and, facing evidence of their group's misdeeds, self-stereotyping predicted group-based guilt while satisfaction and centrality predicted legitimizing the misdeeds. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md)), in place of [LIT-1795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1795.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the direct test of whether identification splits into a self-definition and a caring dimension: it does, and they can work against each other. |
